HEADLINE: Banks tried digital tactics during inquiry
TEXT:
Banks, superannuation funds and insurers ramped up advertising spending to unprecedented levels during the Hayne royal commission last year to counter the negative publicity splashed across newspapers and leading TV news segments generated by the hearings.

Data from the Standard Media Index shows financial services turned to digital sources to boost favourable messages, with money spent on "search" (for instance, increasing their placements in Google's search results) enjoying the largest share of growth across all digital advertising spending in 2018-19 financial year.

SMI tracks spending from four of the five large media agency groups, which sector is spending the money and which medium it is being spent on.

While calendar 2018 may have seen the banks spend big, Hayne's final report, which was delivered in February, saw overall domestic bank ad spend pull back heavily from those record levels. SMI data shows domestic bank spend in the first six months of 2019 plummet 16.8 per cent compared to the same time last year. Insurers increased their spend by 6.3 per cent in the same period.

In the 2018-19 financial year, the financial services industry accounted for a total of 40 per cent of all dollars spent on digital advertising in 2018-19, which ranged from placing branded content on publishing websites such as Junkee and Pedestrian to trying to lift their rankings in Google's search results.

Beyond digital, the financial services industry also spent an extra $34.3 million in 2018-19 on posters and billboards over the previous year.

Pedestrian Group chief executive Matt Rowley said this was partly an effort to place favourable messages away from news covering the grievances exposed by the banking royal commission.

"The big four banks especially found ways to spend away from publishers during the royal commission ... you saw spend move towards things like search and outdoor because I think maybe those banks thought they'd be less likely to be put beside maybe 'challenging' content," he said.

But many traditional players were creeping back to publishing, he said, noting an uptick in briefs coming through at Pedestrian. Pedestrian is owned by Nine, which is also the owner of The Australian Financial Review.

Beyond royal commission damage control, banks, superannuation funds and insurers are battling it out to reach and attract Millennials.

"Financial services clients in the digital space really recognise how important Millennials are to them. They've realised that if you can win the Millennial market, you can win the next 20 or 30 years, if you can hook them into your financial services company as a really important part of their lives," said publisher and co-founder of Junkee Media, Tim Duggan.

"It's been a really healthy market for us, the financial services industry, and looking ahead into 2020, I think that's only going to increase."

He noted "native video" had been on the rise at Junkee, whereby the Millennial news site produces bespoke video content for companies such as Westpac and Qantas Frequent Flyer.

Native content from videos to written explainers comprised 60 per cent of Junkee's revenue, with financial services clients making up a "healthy proportion of that", he said.

HEADLINE: News Corp warns on Facebook, Google media manoeuvres
TEXT:
News Corp is concerned Google and Facebook will play local media companies off against each other in negotiating codes of conduct for business relationships, and wants the government to prohibit the platforms from using any Australian publisher's content until agreements are in place across the board.

The Rupert Murdoch-controlled media business wants the competition watchdog's recommendation for a code of conduct to govern business relationships between digital platforms and local media companies - including how revenue is divided and data is shared - to establish a united front for the Australian sector.

News Corp wants the government to prohibit digital platforms from using any news publisher's content and collecting any data generated from its use "unless all news publishers (or at least the major ones) have negotiated and entered into agreements with that digital platform".

"This prohibition on using content would also include using content which is a rewritten version of any news publisher's original content (regardless of who has rewritten the content) and it should also override the 'fair dealing' exceptions in the Copyright Act to prohibit the indexing of content for search and publishing headlines and snippets," News Corp said in its submission to the Treasury regarding the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's Digital Platforms Inquiry.

The company warned of dangers which would ensue if all publishers were not required to have agreed with Facebook and Google.

"Otherwise, digital platforms will continue to be able to play news publishers off against each other and use negotiations with other news publishers as a negotiating tactic in order to force publishers to 'take it or leave it' in regards to critical issues such as use of and payment for content (including snippets) and use and provision of data."

Google has a bespoke advertising deal with Nine, publisher of The Australian Financial Review. In December 2017, Google and Fairfax Media struck an agreement for the tech giant to sell and market programmatic advertising across mastheads including the Financial Review, The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. Nine merged with Fairfax at the end of 2018.

In early August, Facebook signed 12-month deals with Nine, Seven, Ten, Sky News, Junkee and Pedestrian.TV to create a series of original news and current affairs shows for its video service Facebook Watch.

However, the deals aroused suspicion within the media industry given they were timed a little over a week after the ACCC released its final report and the government began its 12-week consultation process.

Most traditional media companies in Australia, including Nine, favour a code of conduct to govern commercial deals with the digital platforms.

The ACCC's 19-month inquiry found there is an imbalance in bargaining power between local media companies and the digital behemoths, and they are "unavoidable business partners". The ACCC found the imbalance in bargaining power led local media businesses to accept the less favourable terms on offer from Google and Facebook.

Both Google and Facebook have hit out against the code of conduct recommendation. Google's chief executive Sundar Pichai told the Financial Review last week he believed market forces would sort out the company's dealings with media businesses and regulatory intervention was not needed.

News Corp said it would not be difficult to put together a list of major publishers who should be designated as publishers. This includes News Corp Australia, Nine, Seven West Media, The Guardian, ABC and SBS.

It also reiterated comments made in the lobby group Free TV Australia's submission that the ACCC should govern the codes of conduct, not the Australian Communications and Media Authority as recommended in the inquiry's final report.

"As Australia's competition and consumer regulator, the ACCC is responsible for promoting competition and fair trading across all Australian industries and sectors by means of its extensive enforcement and regulatory toolkit," News Corp said.

"The ACCC has unique and extensive expertise in managing relationships in industries characterised by significant imbalances of bargaining power.

"Further, the ACCC's reputation as a credible and effective economic and competition regulator will lend clout to the code of conduct regime."

HEADLINE: Carnegie, Wilson push Nine on Macquarie
TEXT:
Venture capitalist Mark Carnegie and Wilson Asset Management chairman Geoff Wilson are in discussions to see if they can extract a better offer from Nine for the radio broadcaster Macquarie Media.

Mr Carnegie has been widely expected to follow his long-time friend John Singleton and vote in favour of Nine's $1.46 per share offer for the remaining shares in Macquarie it doesn't already own. Mr Singleton accepted the offer on Tuesday, taking Nine's stake to 87.05 per cent, just shy of the 90 per cent it needs to compulsorily sweep up the rest of the shares.

However, sources told The Australian Financial Review, which is owned by Nine, that Mr Carnegie and Mr Wilson have recently begun discussing how they might obtain a better deal through either a higher price or the use of Macquarie's balance of franking credits in the offer.

Mr Carnegie holds a 3.6 per cent stake in the radio broadcaster, home of 2GB and 3AW, while Mr Wilson has built up his share to 4.7 per cent. Should Mr Carnegie decide to take the current offer, Nine will have the amount it needs to buy up the rest of Macquarie's shares.

Nine declined to comment and Macquarie chairman Russell Tate was not available on Sunday. Earlier in September, the independent expert PwC declared Nine's offer fair and reasonable. PwC valued Macquarie between $1.44 and $1.66 a share.

Mr Wilson has been the key agitator on the deal and has been pressing Macquarie's independent directors for a better deal for minority shareholders.

In a letter to the Macquarie board last Sunday, Mr Wilson argued that synergies would save more than the $10 million in costs outlined in the offer. The letter argued that significant revenue synergies had not been included, and that as the deal was currently structured Macquarie shareholders would miss out on $14.4 million in franking credits.

The offer is worth more than 10 times Macquarie's $27.1 million in underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for financial 2019.

Mr Wilson confirmed on Sunday that Macquarie's independent directors had responded to his letter by the 5pm Friday deadline he had set.

"We clearly articulated in detail our concerns about the [independent board committee's] recommendation and the Target Statement re valuation, the use of comparable historical transaction multiples, synergies considered and the failure to be compensated for the franking credit balance of $14.4 million," he said.

"In their reply they said that they have acted in all shareholders' best interests and that they took preparatory steps long in advance of receiving the offer. If that was the case, then it is surprising that they neither kept shareholders informed nor were well prepared to secure a better outcome for minority shareholders."

Nine's takeover offer for Macquarie did not come as a surprise after it acquired 54.5 per cent of Macquarie when its merger with Fairfax Media was completed in December. It had previously acknowledged that discussions had taken place.

"It was also disappointing that they didn't address Macquarie's significant franking credit balance and the opportunistic timing of the offer at a time of depressed earnings which the independent expert considered would return to historical levels," Mr Wilson said.

Key pointsNine has 87pc of Macquarie - not quite enough to allow compulsory acquisition.

Mark Carnegie and Geoff Wilson believe synergy savings justify a higher price.

HEADLINE: US backs Sydney biotech to help curb drug crisis
TEXT:
A biotech start-up that is developing a compound to help limit opioid cravings has won a grant from the US government to run clinical trials and help fight the country's drug crisis.

Kinoxis Therapeutics had already attracted investment from some of Australia's most prominent businessmen. The family offices of ex-Macquarie big wigs Allan Moss and Michael Carapiet, former Toll Holdings CEO Paul Little and AustralianSuper director Jim Craig are among the 20-odd investors in the company - which is hopeful of developing pharmaceuticals to manage cravings for drugs through management of the brain's oxytocin system.

Kinoxis, set up in 2018 and spun out of the University of Sydney, has secured a grant of up to $US4.6 million ($6.8 million) from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, a division of the US National Institutes of Health.

NIH has funded $US945 million in research in fiscal 2019, but the Kinoxis funding is the only one from outside North America.

Dr Michael Bowen, of the Brain and Mind Centre and School of Psychology at the University of Sydney and co-founder of Kinoxis, said it would be many years before any possible drug would be available to the public, but the grant provides major validation of the company's research program.

"One thing that is wonderful about this grant is the validation that it provides, not just to the potential part that our company might play in providing a solution to this global pandemic but it's validation there is a model for biotech start-ups based on good research being done at Australian universities," he told The Australian Financial Review.

"This is testament to the strength of that model and recognition that high-net-worth individuals play. They have been absolutely essential in getting us to where we are today."

Dr Bowen, who also works with the Lambert Initiative for Cannabinoid Therapeutics, said the initial funding of $US2.8 million will help the group complete its final efficacy testing.

Kinoxis CEO Hugh Alsop said the award helps accelerate the development of its lead compound, KNX100, into human clinical studies slated for next year. "Being able to work collaboratively with NIDA on this project is a huge plus for our team, given they conduct or fund over two-thirds of the worlds addiction research," he said.

"Kinoxis is a great example of the translation of science from research into a company - a process under continual scrutiny as Australia attempts to lift itself up global rankings."

Australia is ranked 22nd on the World's Global Innovation Index 2019, falling two spots this year, with Austria and Iceland both climbing higher.

Mr Alsop added the award is recognition of the potential to successfully manage opioid withdrawal symptoms and help curb the opioid crisis.

The US opioid epidemic has hit new heights with Purdue Pharma - the drug maker of OxyContin accused of fuelling the crisis - filing for bankruptcy in September. Forbes has estimated the owners of Purdue - the Sackler family - are worth $US13 billion.

Purdue is being sued by a number of US states over its role in the liberal prescribing of OxyContin. While the drug has been marketed as a safer form of narcotic pain killer, the abuse of OxyContin has ballooned into a major health crisis in the US and Australia.

Dr Bowen said in Australia opioids are killing three people every day - mostly from accidental overdose - while the number of opioid overdoses has quadrupled over the past two decades in the US.

As addiction expert Dr Bowen said: "It's impossible to not look at those companies and say they have not had a big part to play in the current crisis."

He added that Kinoxis' lead compound is showing promise in other highly addictive drugs: meth amphetamine, alcohol, nicotine and cocaine.

Total capital invested so far in Kinoxis has reached $5.12 million, with the University of Sydney and Uniseed (a venture fund operating at the Universities of Melbourne, Queensland, Sydney and New South Wales, and the CSIRO, each controlling 18 per cent of the company.

HEADLINE: Blackmore dreams of a takeover from China
TEXT:
The biggest shareholder in Blackmores says the vitamin group is looking for a potential joint venture partner in China to help re-invigorate its business in that country, and concedes a takeover offer from a Chinese entity is a distinct possibility at some point.

Marcus Blackmore, who holds 23.1 per cent of Blackmores, has just handed the reins to new chief executive Alastair Symington after six months of running the day-to-day operations himself as interim chief executive following the departure of the company's previous boss, Richard Henfrey.

"It's top of the mind all the time," Mr Blackmore said of the possibility of a takeover offer for Blackmores.

The corporate interest in Australian consumer goods firms was reinforced again two weeks ago when the $25 billion China Mengniu Dairy Company made a $1.5 billion takeover offer for infant formula company Bellamy's.

The Bellamy's offer triggered a jump in the share price of other consumer goods companies that had a big focus on China, including Blackmores, which jumped 9.4 per cent on the day.

Blackmores' big rival in vitamins, Swisse, was itself acquired by a Chinese company in a two-step buyout in 2015 and 2016 - Health & Happiness, previously known as Biostime International, paid $1.7 billion to buy it.

Blackmores set up a joint venture with Indonesian pharmaceutical and nutrition company Kalbe Farma in 2016 to expand into Indonesia.

"It's turned out to be really good," Mr Blackmore said. Indonesian sales had risen 90 per cent in 2018-19, albeit from a low base.

He said Blackmores hadn't yet found the right partner but a similar model would work well to enable better penetration of the complex Chinese market, which had been a goldmine for the company in 2015 and 2016 before a sales slump in 2018-19.

"We're enthusiastic about finding a partner in China. We're going down that path. We haven't got that partner at the moment and we will continue looking".

Blackmores' overall sales to consumers in China were down 14 per cent for 2018-19 because of changes to e-commerce regulations and smaller daigou traders abandoning their previous robust business model of buying vitamins in Australia from retailers and selling them online in China.

China is a large chunk of Blackmores annual sales of $600 million-plus.

Mr Blackmore said Mr Symington, who had been in the CEO seat for a few days, was making a strong impression.

He had been based in Dubai with global cosmetics group Coty, which owns brands such as Max Factor and Cover Girl. "At this stage, I am very impressed by his management style. He listens, then he makes up his own mind," Mr Blackmore said.

"He's been extremely well accepted. All the signs are very good."

Mr Symington, who grew up in Melbourne, has been out and about meeting customers in his first few days, including Mr Blackmore's local pharmacy on Sydney's northern beaches.

Mr Blackmore, a veteran Financial Review Rich Lister, became interim boss after the departure in February of Henfrey, following a dive in profits.

Mr Blackmore's 23.1 per cent stake was worth $338 million at Blackmores' closing share price of $84.29 on Friday.

The shares soared to as high as $220 in early January 2016 on super-profits from a sharp jump in Chinese demand.

Mr Blackmore's stake would be crucial in any takeover tilt by an outsider.

Many Chinese companies have had the luxury of a big war chest through shareholdings by state-owned enterprises. The Bellamy's Australia suitor China Mengniu Dairy Co is part-owned by Chinese state-owned enterprise China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Corporation (COFCO).

Mr Blackmore said Chinese consumers loved the "clean and green" image of products manufactured here. "We do know Chinese people prefer Australian-made products," he added.

HEADLINE: Economists challenged by a world that's on fire
TEXT:
No matter how finely calibrated the models of Australia's leading economists, there's just no way they can calculate the cumulative impact of risks like the latest Trump twitter tantrum, another Brexit stumble, or an attack on Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure.

The world is a risky place, and the outlook for Australia's sluggish economy remains captive to events well beyond our shores - and our control.

The halcyon days of the Great Moderation and well established norms of international politics and trade are over, replaced by a chaotic evolution of a new regime marked by unconventional monetary policy, resurgent superpower rivalries, and an attempt to rewrite the rules of the rules-based global order.

No economist - not matter how many post-nominals they have - can truly capture the economic impact of an uncertain world on our small, open economy. They have been trained to think of a world of equilibrium - a fantasy far detached from the world of disequilibrium we see before us.

The trade war between the US and China has been the trigger for much of the concern about the fragility of the global economy.

Yes, it has tangible economic consequences that can be modelled, but it's the intangible impact on sentiment in the real economy and financial markets that is much harder to quantify.

It's cold comfort that standing between a possible deal between the two giants of the global economy is Donald Trump and another ill-timed and ill-tempered tweet. It highlights the absurdity of trade policy being made on the run and communicated via a social media platform.

It has a direct bearing on Australia. China looms large in Australia's economic calculus given its dominant role as our largest trade partner.

But the latest readings of China's economic pulse have been weak. That not only reflects the impact of the trade war on activity in China's factories, but Beijing's attempts to de-risk the economy by avoiding the temptation to revert back to debt-fuelled stop-go growth policies of the past.

The uncertainty of China's economic relations with the US is a complication for Beijing as its looks to deliver a doubling of the economy by 2020 and navigate its way beyond the middle income trap.

Australia's and Beijing's past beliefs about the likely trajectory for China's economy are being reshaped by a trade dispute that is targeting China's access to key growth-enabling technologies like semiconductors - a risk that was unthought of a couple of years ago.

The uncertainty unleashed by the "crash or crash-through" tactics of the White House also looms large over US monetary policy.

President Trump wants lower US rates and is prepared to use the trade war - and ad hominem attacks and insults like "boneheads" - to get what he wants.

Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell has cut rates but has stood firm in not signalling the massive easing in policy that Trump demands.

But how does an economist model US rates - and their impact on global growth and markets - when the President seems prepared to sacrifice growth now for a monetary policy sugar hit later on?

Add in the circus that is Brexit, the risk it poses to Europe's economy, protests on the streets of Hong Kong, and the exposed vulnerability of the world's energy infrastructure, and it's clear modelling the future is becoming an endeavour fraught with more hazard than ever.

HEADLINE: Canberra cottons on to credit crunch
TEXT:
Bankers, who have spent the past 18 months shielding themselves from a barrage of unrelenting and scathing criticism, could scarcely believe their ears last week as senior politicians abruptly changed tack last week and tried to cajole them into lending for the sake of the economy.

But the sudden shift in the political winds will have left James Shipton, who runs the country's top corporate regulator, feeling decidedly uncomfortable, particularly after ASIC's controversial decision to appeal Justice Nye Perram's judgment in the "wagyu and shiraz case".

Speaking in New York on Wednesday, Prime Minister Scott Morrison warned that an ill-judged and heavy-handed response to the Hayne royal commission could choke off the supply of credit to the economy.

"While it's important to address those conduct issues with the banks, we must be very, very careful that we don't lead our banks into a place where they've been overly sheepish, and that can really cut off the opportunities that we would otherwise have," he said.

Although he didn't explicitly point the finger at regulators, Morrison noted there had been an "instinctiveness" in the wake of the Hayne royal commission to adopt overly onerous lending standards, that could cause lending to dry up.

The Prime Minister's comments were seconded the very next day by his Treasurer, Josh Frydenberg, who cautioned regulators against adopting an overly officious interpretation of responsible lending rules, because this risked penalising "hard-working families" trying to get a housing loan and could damage the economy.

"It's in everyone's interest that the aspirations of hard-working families are not collateral damage in this regulatory process," Frydenberg said.

"If responsible lending laws are applied too stringently, they will also negatively impact consumer behaviour."

Unlike the Prime Minister, Frydenberg alluded to ASIC's decision to appeal the Federal Court's decision on banks' responsible lending obligations.

In August, Westpac secured a stunning victory in the landmark case over responsible lending, with the Federal Court dismissing ASIC's case, and instead ordering it to pay the bank's $5 million or so in legal costs.

"Common sense dictates that a sensible balance needs to be struck because an unduly restrictive application of those obligations can do as much harm as an overly lax one", Frydenberg said.

He also warned that the supply of credit would be reduced and its cost would rise if bankers were forced to shoulder full responsibility for avoiding soured loans.

"The value of personal responsibility and personal accountability must remain central to our society and if the pendulum swings too far in the abrogation of these values, then it will inevitably reduce the availability of credit and increase its price".

Of course, it's hardly surprising that both the Prime Minister and the Treasurer have decided that they need to change their rhetoric on the banks.

The economy expanded by only 1.4 per cent over the year to June, its slowest annual growth in a decade. And it's clear that banks' increased reluctance to lend - both to small businesses and for home loans - has acted as a big brake on economic activity.

The most recent Reserve Bank figures show that lending to business grew at 3.9 per cent in the year to July 2019, down from the more robust pace of 5.2 per cent six months earlier. (Interestingly, this slowdown in business lending is occurring at a time when almost every bank in the country has adopted a strategy of boosting their lending to small businesses.)

Meanwhile, lending for housing grew at a very modest 3.3 per cent in the year to July 2019, down from a 4.4 per cent clip six months earlier.

And even though home loan lending has picked up following the Reserve Bank's decision to cut interest rates in June and July - with a further cut expected on Tuesday - bankers complain that ASIC's decision to appeal against the "wagyu and shiraz" responsible lending case means there will be no clarity over their responsible lending obligations for at least a year.

ASIC's position is that when it comes to assessing home loans, bankers should pay close attention to the borrower's historical spending pattern, rather than relying on a frugal benchmark - the household expenditure measure - to estimate living expenses.

Justice Perram was quick to point to the flaw in ASIC's argument, saying that "the mere fact that there are living expenses is not necessarily relevant to whether a consumer will be unable to comply with their loan obligations because it is always possible that some of the living expenses might be foregone by the consumer in order to meet the repayments."

By way of illustration, he noted: "I may eat wagyu beef every day, washed down with the finest shiraz, but if I really want my new home, I can make do on much more modest fare."

But while lower interest rates appears to have sparked a recovery in home lending, banks remain extremely cautious about lending to small business due to the lingering uncertainty over their responsible lending obligations.

Banks are now much more reluctant to make loans to small businesses using the family home as security, because this long-standing practice is now seen as politically sensitive.

Bankers are also highly conscious of the risk that these small business loans will subsequently be deemed to be home loans, and consequently be subject to responsible lending rules.

That's because for small business owners, there is a lot of overlap between personal and business affairs.

This financial fluidity causes bankers to worry that what they considered to be a small business loan secured by property could subsequently be deemed to be a home loan, which would be subject to stringent responsible lending rules.

"ASIC doesn't believe there is any ambiguity", one senior banker said. "The whole industry believes there is".

The increased difficulty that small businesses face in obtaining finance following the Hayne royal commission is a major concern in Canberra because it reduces the Reserve Bank's ability to boost activity by cutting interest rates.

Already, the move by the banks to adopt tougher home loan lending standards has triggered a noticeable slowdown in property construction.

Canberra is deeply concerned that if banks continue to shy away from small business lending, the cracks in the economy will become wider and deeper. And that is why, for the first time in almost two years, our political leaders are now siding with the banks - who for months have argued that the tougher regulations are causing a credit crunch, especially for small businesses - rather than the regulators, who have consistently dismissed the banks' claims as "myths".

HEADLINE: Challenge to ASIC may prove 'embarrassing'
TEXT:
The corporate watchdog's new product intervention power has been challenged in a bold legal move that could prove a significant loss for the regulator, according to legal experts.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission used its product intervention power, which allows it to ban financial and credit products that may result in significant consumer detriment, in early September. It banned a certain model of payday lending.

But Cigno, the only lender impacted by the order, has appealed it in the Federal Court in the latest challenge faced by ASIC as it works to show its post-Hayne enforcement teeth.

"We don't know yet, but if it turns out [Cigno's] allegation is well-founded, it will be embarrassing for ASIC and a significant blow to its credibility," Allens' senior regulator counsel Michael Mathieson said.

"If I were ASIC, I'd want to be absolutely sure that [the first intervention order] wouldn't be vulnerable to attack," he said, especially with regulators under pressure.

ASIC last month lost its now-infamous "Wagyu and shiraz" responsible lending case against Westpac, and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority came off second-best in its highly publicised court battle with IOOF.

Hall & Wilcox special counsel Vince Battaglia said it was rare for ASIC to receive a new power and exercise it, only to have its first use of that power challenged in court.

"Too often, ASIC's regulatory interventions are asserted without challenge," he said.

Mr Battaglia said most businesses "simply concede to ASIC's demands" as they are "intent on managing legal and reputation risk".

This could become commonplace, however, as more Hayne laws are passed.

"New legislation such as this will continue to be subject to judicial review in coming years," said Liam Hennessy, a senior associate in financial services compliance at King & Wood Mallesons.

But Cigno may have a battle on its hands in court. ASIC ran a consultation period on the order, as it is legally required to when banning products, and only two out of the 35 submissions it received objected to the order.

Cigno's case argues ASIC wrongly classed the payday lending model as a financial product and questions whether its associate company Gold Silver's credit facility causes financial detriment.

Mr Hennessy warned that the product intervention powers law was "untested and complex legislation".

"It's challenging to run a case on such a technical interpretation of the law," he said.

Both ASIC and Cigno declined to comment.

For consumer law advocates who have long pushed for the abolition of this payday-lending business model, ASIC's use of the intervention power was not contentious.

"For us, this was an 'open and shut' case for how the product intervention powers should work. This company's behaviour has just been shocking and egregious," the CEO of Financial Counselling Australia, Fiona Guthrie, said.

"I wouldn't say ASIC is stumbling - I would say Cigno has nothing to lose, its back is against the world and this is its last stand."

She added that should Cigno prove successful in its appeal, the law around the product intervention powers should be strengthened.

"If these powers are found not to be adequate to rein in behaviour as appalling as this then we need urgent law reform.

"If [Cigno's appeal] means that every time ASIC tries to use these new and important powers, it is going to be challenged this way ... we may [also] need further law reform in that regard."

The regulator already unsuccessfully tried to ban this particular payday-lending business model, losing a 2014 Federal Court case against two Gold Coast-based lenders.

HEADLINE: Combet calls for rethink on Ralston
TEXT:
Industry Super Australia has called on the Morrison government to reconsider the appointment of Deborah Ralston to the retirement income inquiry because she has lobbied for "voluntary" superannuation for low-income earners.

Dr Ralston wrote to Treasurer Josh Frydenberg in July to propose that the inquiry consider allowing lower-income earners to receive super in wages because increasing super to 12 per cent would force them to forgo too much money.

ISA chairman and former Australian Council of Trade Unions secretary, Greg Combet, slammed the idea as "a dangerous proposal that will see vulnerable workers slugged more in taxes only to end up with less money in retirement".

"We have serious concerns about Dr Ralston's ability to conduct an independent review of Australia's retirement income system when it appears she opposes the very premise the system was built on, which is compulsory superannuation," he said.

"In light of the need for the review's findings to be unimpeachable, we believe the Treasurer should reflect upon the appropriateness of Dr Ralston's appointment to the panel."

Dr Ralston is chairman of the SMSF Association but has stepped aside while the review is conducted. Her letter to the Treasurer, on behalf of the Alliance for a Fairer Retirement System, was sent in the same month that Liberal senator Andrew Bragg proposed allowing those earning less than $50,000 to opt out of compulsory super contributions.

ISA analysis found that Senator Bragg's proposal would result in those on $50,000 a year being hit with a higher income tax bill of $1710 a year, a rise of almost $1000.

"Taking away compulsory super for low-income earners would be bad for the country and bad for the economy," Mr Combet said. "Not only would it condemn some of our most vulnerable Australians to poverty in retirement - everyone would end up paying in the long run because we'd have to support more people on the pension."

However, the Grattan Institute and National Seniors Australia have given conditional support to Dr Ralston's proposal.

Brendan Coates, the household finances program director at the Grattan Institute, said the super guarantee should not increase to 12 per cent because the existing rate of 9.5 per cent was already adequate to maintain living standards into retirement.

If the increase to 12 per cent went ahead, he said a "second best" solution was making some portion of the compulsory super guarantee voluntary.

"It's clear that super comes at the cost of wages and some lower income earners are probably saving for a higher standard in retirement than what they would have beforehand [in their working life]," he said.

"Rather than making super voluntary from the first dollar, the review may well consider whether super contributions beyond some minimum level should be voluntary."

But he said "we should pretty careful in unwinding the compulsory element of super", warning that making super voluntary from the first dollar earned may result in people not saving for retirement and relying fully on the age pension.

The review has not been asked to make policy recommendations, but rather to give a stocktake of the retirement income system. Dr Ralston's fellow panellists are retired Treasury official Mike Callaghan and Future Fund board member Carolyn Kay.

HEADLINE: Carter's faith restored from dot com's ashes
TEXT:
Monday fundie IFM veteran's small caps strategy still delivers.

An eye for growth stocks demands a willingness to pay more for high-octane earnings than a value stock demands. But there's another aspect to growth investing that value investors don't talk about: the uncertainty.

"It's not that it's difficult to do the valuation, it's just that the range of potential outcomes is very wide," says Neil Carter, global co-head of equities at IFM Investors with Aidan Puddy. Carter also has direct responsibility for IFM's small caps strategy, which has zeroed in on growth names such as Afterpay - which it bought at $2.45 - to underpin returns.

"The difference between your bear case, your base case and your upside case can be incredibly wide. With a traditional earnings-based multiple valuation you're probably within 10 or 20 per cent of the right number. It's a very narrow range."

After leaving management consulting and obtaining an MBA at Insead in France, Carter started out as a media analyst in 1997 at ABN Amro in the UK with oversight of ten FTSE 100 stocks. It was a hot sector at the time.

"The great thing about the media is they love writing about the media. There was always plenty of news flow, so it was actually really good," he says. "I went right through the boom and bust of the dot com period and media was the closest thing to internet that existed."

While there, he covered WPP. ("Martin Sorrell's quite a character," Carter says, "he could be pretty interesting at times.") And while it's a different market these days, 20 years ago it was not uncommon for an analyst to be torched for unfavourable coverage.

"I did get called in by the CFO of Reuters one time who basically asked me to 'please explain', because I had published the last four notes, all of them with hold recommendations, and as soon as you read the text it was clear the hold was really a sell."

Carter moved to Australia in 2002 to set up a telco, media and technology hedge fund, but it suffered from a lack of distribution. Now at IFM, probably the second-largest Australian listed equities manager after Vanguard, he has a different and impossibly broad perspective.

"I sit on the investment committee and I see the way our infrastructure guys model and value businesses. For them, the cash flows are so predictable you can model out 30, 40 years with quite a good level of certainty.

"Then the argument becomes about 'what WACC (weighted average cost of capital) should I be applying?' 'What's the discount rate for these cashflows?' But if you're in a global tech start-up, the profile of just growing the top line can be highly uncertain. It's that level of uncertainty which makes the valuation as much art as science."

The past few years have seen active managers struggle from fee compression and a growing preference for passive, causing fund managers to close their doors. But it's been even more painful for value styles given the outperformance of growth.

"If you're a traditional dyed-in-the-wool value manager, you've really struggled," Carter acknowledges. "Take effectively a shrinking revenue pool for managers, and you combine that with a bunch of value managers with very poor performance, and you end up with a bloodbath."

He agrees the capital intensive industries where you have to invest heavily to hopefully make a 10 per cent return are incredibly challenged, and the companies which have done well are capital-light.

"And if you're a traditional value manager, you haven't been able to see past the fact it hasn't got a single-digit P/E - can't touch that."

Carter's small caps strategy has returned more than 5 per cent a year above the benchmark since inception. "The way technology has shifted, it has meant that the opportunity for shareholder value creation is just enormous," he says.

IFM still owns Afterpay, but the fund manager remains keen to find stocks that offer the benefit of industry tailwinds, a global opportunity, capital light business models and a strong competitive advantage.

Appen, Nearmap, Audinate and Megaport come to mind, he suggests, but even great stocks get over-valued and the team actively trades core positions. "It's important not to sell winners too early," he cautions, "so we constantly re-evaluate our investment thesis."

At $42 billion in equities, the industry fund is asserting itself in the environmental, social and governance realm. "I know it almost seems a bit trite now, everyone's talking about it. It's very important. We think it makes good business sense that you consider all environmental, social and governance risks. There's a whole bunch of data that suggests for example that board diversity helps drive superior share price performance."

IFM backs the 30 per cent club (30 per cent representation of women on ASX 200 boards) and has written to all the companies with zero or one female director proposing ways for them to tap into candidate pools.

"The typical push-back is 'we just can't find any women with the right skill set'. Well, you're looking in the wrong place," says Carter. "I won't name names but we will be voting against management teams who are actually obstructive."

While it works with the Australian Council of Superannuation Investors, IFM can and sometimes does take a different view.

"If you're not looking after your workforce and you're mistreating them, you're going to have high staff turnover," he says. "That's going to end up driving greater costs into your business.

"If you're not respecting your customers, if you're not interacting well with regulators, if you're environmental controls aren't good. We're very strong on the issue of safety. We won't accept companies with poor safety records, we don't think anyone should die because they've turned up for work.

"Good safety is a sign of good management, good systems and poor safety is both morally unacceptable and it's bad for business."

The end of shareholder primacy as declared by Jamie Dimon and James Gorman early this year does not sound that provocative to the fund manager.

"It's become this topic of conversation which is dead right, but the public debate is almost playing catch-up with what's happening in markets."

Carter started investing with his father in the 1980s when the UK was privatising assets. "He lent me money for the first one which might have been British Airways, and we made some money and rolled that into the next one. So Dad and I went on this little adventure of stagging Margaret Thatcher's privatisations," he recalls.

He is one of five boys, but the only one who caught the investing bug.

"When I talk to fund managers who have been around a long time, I think there's a lot of frustration with some of the industry trends that we're seeing here in Australia and a lot of people, they kind of think it's a bit unfair, because the world has changed, the revenue pots that used to exist are either shrinking or disappearing."

His advice is to accept it and get on with it. "Face the new reality, and build products and services for the new world."

The reality is that's much more global in focus, it's lower fee, "but potentially much bigger FUM numbers", referring to funds under management. "And that can work if you cut your cloth appropriately, you've got the right cost structure, you've got good systems, you can still survive and hopefully thrive."

Carter's discussion with The Australian Financial Review comes just after the attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and the Hong Kong protests. IFM has a Hong Kong office and took advice as the situation escalated.

"A lot of the expat investment community have generally been reporting that it's overblown and the news media made more of it than is the case, but the security advisors that we've consulted suggest that's quite a common view when you're inside one of these situations," he says of the instinct to minimise.
